How a dependency's license change reaches your lockfile

Nobody chooses to accept a relicense. It arrives as a version bump: an automated PR from Dependabot or Renovate, or a routine npm update, carrying release notes about performance and bug fixes — and, unannounced in the diff a reviewer actually reads, a different license field in the new version's own package.json.

Why Dependabot and Renovate don't catch it

Both tools solve a different problem well: they watch a registry for a newer version and open a pull request with the version delta, changelog, and a compatibility signal. Neither diffs the license field between the version you have and the version they're proposing — it isn't part of what either was built to compare. A license change rides along inside an otherwise-routine version PR with nothing calling it out.

Four times this actually happened

ProjectFromToDate
MongoDB ServerAGPL-3.0SSPL-1.02018-10-16
Elasticsearch & KibanaApache-2.0SSPL-1.0 / Elastic License2021-01-14
TerraformMPL-2.0BUSL-1.12023-08-10
RedisBSD-3-ClauseSSPLv1 / RSALv22024-03-20

Each of these is a widely used dependency, not an obscure one. The Terraform change alone drove the OpenTF Manifesto to more than 33,000 GitHub stars within a month and produced OpenTofu; the Redis change produced Valkey, forked and backed by the Linux Foundation within days. None of that visibility retroactively protected the projects that had already merged the version bump before anyone noticed.

Generating a snapshot per ecosystem

Node / npm — reads each installed package's own package.json, no network call:

node cli.mjs snapshot --out baseline.json

Python — pip-licenses already emits JSON; this reshapes its field names to match:

pip-licenses --format=json | \
  jq '[.[] | {name: .Name, version: .Version, license: .License}]' \
  > baseline.json

Go — go-licenses emits a header-less import path,license URL,license name CSV, which the tool reads directly (the last column is used as the license):

go-licenses csv ./... > baseline.csv

Rust — cargo-license's JSON already uses name/version/license:

cargo license --json > baseline.json

Wiring it into CI as a gate

Commit a reviewed baseline snapshot once, then compare against it on every PR that touches the lockfile:

- name: Check for dependency license drift
  run: |
    npm ci
    node ventures/license-drift-check/cli.mjs snapshot --out /tmp/current.json
    node ventures/license-drift-check/cli.mjs diff license-baseline.json /tmp/current.json

The command exits non-zero the moment any package's license changed since the baseline, and 0 on a clean run or a change you've explicitly accepted with --ignore. Nothing here decides whether a given change is acceptable — it makes the change visible in the one place code review already happens, instead of silent inside a version bump.

What the family label does and doesn't mean

Each license is bucketed into permissive, copyleft, or source-available by matching well-known keywords in the license string — a skim aid, not a legal determination. The one mix-up worth naming explicitly: colloquial "BSL" almost always means the source-available Business Source License (SPDX BUSL-1.1, the one Terraform, Sentry, and CockroachDB use) — not the fully permissive Boost Software License (SPDX BSL-1.0). The tool disambiguates on the version digit; read the actual license text before relying on either label.

Common questions

Is colloquial "BSL" the same license as SPDX BSL-1.0?

No, and mixing them up runs in both directions. Colloquial "BSL" almost always means the source-available Business Source License (SPDX BUSL-1.1), the one Terraform, Sentry, and CockroachDB use. SPDX BSL-1.0 is the unrelated, fully permissive Boost Software License.

Does this tool decide whether a license change is compliant or safe to accept?

No. It reports that a package's license string differs from a snapshot you captured earlier, and buckets the before and after into a public, well-known family as a skim aid. Whether a given change is acceptable for your project is a decision for you or your counsel, not this tool.

Can I use this if my project isn't on npm?

Yes. The diff engine reads a generic JSON array of {name, version, license} objects, or CSV with a name/version/license header, so pip-licenses, go-licenses, and cargo-license output all work with the commands above — only the snapshot command that scans node_modules directly is npm-specific.

No warranty. This page and the tool it documents report a factual difference between two snapshots you supply. Nothing here is legal advice about any license, and the family labels are an informational keyword match, not a legal opinion. Verify with counsel before relying on it. Back to the tool.

LICENSE DRIFT CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Did a dependency's license just change under you?

Paste a baseline snapshot (last known-good) and a current snapshot of your dependency tree's declared licenses, and this reports exactly which packages' license changed since then — not their version, their license. Terraform (→ BUSL-1.1, 2023), Redis (→ SSPL/RSAL, 2024), Elasticsearch (→ SSPL, 2021), and MongoDB (→ SSPL, 2018) all relicensed a widely used open-source project this way, and a routine dependency bump is exactly how each change reached an existing user.

Nothing is uploaded. The text you paste is parsed in this browser and never leaves your device.

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file — and it can capture a snapshot from your local node_modules directly (a browser cannot read your filesystem):

node cli.mjs snapshot --out baseline.json          # commit this once, after review
npm ci                                             # ...time passes, dependencies update...
node cli.mjs snapshot --out current.json
node cli.mjs diff baseline.json current.json       # human-readable, exit 1 if anything changed
node cli.mjs diff baseline.json current.json --json
node cli.mjs diff baseline.json current.json --ignore left-pad,is-odd

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. It reads only local files: no network call, ever.

Common questions

Why doesn't Dependabot or Renovate already catch this?

They watch for new versions and open a pull request with the version delta and release notes. Neither diffs the license field between what you had and what you're about to get, so a routine version bump can carry a license change straight into a merged PR with nothing flagging it.

Is this legal advice about whether a license change matters to me?

No. It reports a factual difference — the license string changed from A to B — and buckets each into a public, well-known family (permissive, copyleft, source-available) as a skim aid, not a legal opinion. Whether a specific change matters to your specific use is a question for you or your counsel.

What format do the snapshots need to be in?

A JSON array of {name, version, license} objects — exactly what node cli.mjs snapshot writes from a local node_modules folder — or plain CSV with a name/version/license header, which is what pip-licenses --format=json (via a one-line jq conversion) or go-licenses csv already produce. See the docs page for exact commands per ecosystem.

Is my dependency data uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses the snapshots you paste entirely in your own browser and never sends them anywhere. The CLI reads only local files — no network call, ever.

← License Drift Check

License Drift Check vs. FOSSA

FOSSA is a hosted software composition analysis (SCA) platform. It connects to your repositories, continuously scans your dependency tree, tells you what license each dependency carries right now, checks that against a policy you configure (for example, block strong copyleft in a proprietary codebase), and can generate an SBOM or fail a build on a policy violation. It is a genuinely useful, always-on system for an organization that wants license compliance enforced across every repository without anyone checking by hand.

That is not this tool's job. License Drift Check parses two point-in-time snapshots you paste — a baseline and a current one — and reports exactly which packages' license changed, were added, or were removed between them. Nothing is uploaded, there is no account, no policy engine, and no memory once you close the tab.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What license does every dependency in my codebase carry right now, continuously, across my whole org? FOSSA — that needs an ongoing connected scan and a policy engine, which a stateless browser page never does.
I have a baseline snapshot and today's snapshot — did any package's license change between them? License Drift Check — paste both, get the exact list of changed, added, and removed packages, no signup, nothing leaves your device.
I want a build to fail automatically when a dependency violates my license policy. FOSSA's policy engine — this tool reports a diff, it does not enforce a rule about which licenses are acceptable.
My dependency tree is private and I don't want to connect an account or upload it just to check for a relicensing event. License Drift Check — the browser page never makes a network request, and the CLI reads only local files.

The two are not substitutes. A team that wants continuous, policy-driven license enforcement across every repository and every contributor needs a hosted platform like FOSSA — a page that only looks at whatever you paste into it, once, cannot do that job. A developer who already has two snapshots and wants to know what changed between them, without connecting a repository or accepting a policy engine's opinion of what is acceptable, does not need an account to get that answer.

Common questions

Should I use License Drift Check or FOSSA?

They answer different questions. FOSSA is a hosted software composition analysis (SCA) platform: it connects to your repositories, continuously scans every dependency, tells you what license each one carries right now, checks that against a policy you configure (for example, block copyleft in a proprietary codebase), and can generate SBOMs and block a build on a violation. License Drift Check is a free tool with no account and no connection: you paste two point-in-time snapshots of your dependency tree's declared licenses — a baseline and a current one — and it reports exactly which packages' license changed, were added, or were removed between them. FOSSA tells you the state today; this tool tells you what moved since last time. If you want continuous policy enforcement across a whole org, FOSSA's job is not one this page tries to do. If you already have two snapshots and want the diff before connecting anything, that is what this tool is for.

Does FOSSA already catch a license change on its own?

FOSSA's own product describes continuous scanning and policy checks against the license each dependency currently carries, which will flag a newly-scanned dependency that now violates your policy. What it is built to answer is the current state against a rule you set, not a side-by-side diff of exactly which packages changed license since an earlier snapshot you choose yourself — the four events this tool's README documents (MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Terraform, Redis) are exactly the case where the policy did not change, only the license did, underneath a routine version bump.

Is FOSSA free?

FOSSA offers a free tier for public open-source projects. Scanning private repositories, team seats, policy enforcement across an organization, and SBOM export at scale are paid tiers. License Drift Check has no account and nothing that bills at any tier — it is a free static page and a zero-dependency CLI, for public or private dependency trees alike, with no per-repository or per-seat cost.

Is this page affiliated with FOSSA?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by FOSSA, Inc. FOSSA is named here only to describe what this tool is and is not, based on FOSSA's own public product description.

vs-manually-rechecking-licenses.html.text:
← License Drift Check

License Drift Check vs. manually re-checking each dependency's license

Manually re-checking is the default method, because it needs no tool: after a dependency update, open each package that shows a version bump in the lockfile diff and read its license field yourself. It works when the diff touches one or two packages you already recognize. It stops working at the scale a routine npm update or pip install -U actually produces, because a version bump carries no signal about whether the license moved with it — a patch release and a relicense look identical in a diff that only shows version numbers.

PackageBaselineCurrentVerdict
left-pad1.3.0, MITnot touched this updatestable
stable-lib2.1.0, Apache-2.02.2.0, Apache-2.0version bump only
infra-tool1.9.0, MPL-2.02.0.0, BUSL-1.1license changed

Eyeballing the lockfile diff, stable-lib and infra-tool both look like the same kind of event: a routine minor-to-major version bump. Nothing in either diff line says which one also changed its declared license. Pasted into this tool, the two snapshots resolve to one finding: infra-tool changed from MPL-2.0 (copyleft) to BUSL-1.1 (source-available); stable-lib is reported unchanged. This is the exact shape of HashiCorp's real 2023 Terraform relicense — MPL-2.0 to BUSL-1.1 — which also arrived inside a version bump nobody flagged in time. Merging on "the diff looked like an ordinary release" is exactly the mechanism that carried it, and the other three events this tool's README documents, into projects that never chose to accept the new terms.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I have last month's dependency list and today's — did any package's license change between them? License Drift Check — paste both, get the exact list of changed, added, and removed packages in one click, no signup.
My lockfile diff shows a dozen packages bumped — which ones do I need to open and re-read the license for? License Drift Check — it names exactly the ones whose license field changed; manual re-checking means opening all twelve to find out.
A package's version number jumped from 1.x to 2.0 — does that mean the license changed too? Neither method can tell from the version number alone; a major bump and a relicense are independent facts. This tool reads the license field itself rather than inferring anything from semver.
I want to be sure a specific package I already accepted a license change for doesn't keep flagging every run. License Drift Check — the CLI and the browser page both accept an ignore list; a manual check has no equivalent memory across updates.

Neither method is wrong about the small case: one dependency updated, one page to open, a person can read that correctly every time. The gap opens exactly where a real dependency tree already makes manual re-checking hardest — a lockfile diff with a dozen or more version bumps in it, most of them genuinely routine, and no signal in the diff itself pointing at the one that is not. That is precisely when "the bumps all looked ordinary" and "every one of their licenses is still what it was last time" stop being the same sentence, and it is the gap this tool exists to close.

Common questions

What does manually re-checking dependency licenses get wrong?

A lockfile diff or a Dependabot/Renovate PR shows which packages bumped version — it does not show which one's license field changed, because a license is metadata, not a code diff line. Checking by hand means opening every bumped package's own registry or GitHub page, one at a time, and reading its license yourself. At two or three dependencies that is realistic. At the dozens a routine npm update or pip install -U touches, a person reads the ones that look risky — a major version bump, an unfamiliar name — and skips the ones that look routine, which is exactly where a relicense hides: nothing about a version number says whether the license changed with it.

Can you give a concrete example?

A baseline snapshot has three packages: left-pad 1.3.0 (MIT), infra-tool 1.9.0 (MPL-2.0), and stable-lib 2.1.0 (Apache-2.0). After an update, left-pad is untouched, stable-lib bumps to 2.2.0 still under Apache-2.0, and infra-tool bumps to 2.0.0 — now under BUSL-1.1. The lockfile diff shows two version bumps, both looking like ordinary releases; nothing distinguishes the one that also changed license from the one that did not. Pasted into this tool, the two snapshots resolve to one finding: infra-tool changed license from MPL-2.0 (copyleft) to BUSL-1.1 (source-available); stable-lib is reported unchanged. This is the exact shape of HashiCorp's real 2023 Terraform relicense, MPL-2.0 to BUSL-1.1, which also arrived inside a routine version bump.

Is this tool just automating something obvious?

Reading one package's license field is obvious once you already know to open that specific package's page. What manual re-checking gets wrong is coverage: deciding, for every single package a lockfile diff touched, to actually go open its page and read the license string, not just skim the version number and the changelog for anything alarming. A dependency tree with dozens of packages updating in one PR makes that full sweep exactly the kind of bookkeeping a person under time pressure to merge skips — which is why the four relicensing events this tool's README documents all reached existing users through a routine bump nobody re-checked.

Does this replace reading the new license text?

No. It replaces the step of noticing that a package's license string changed at all. Once it names infra-tool as changed from MPL-2.0 to BUSL-1.1, you still need to read what BUSL-1.1 actually permits for your use — this tool's family label (permissive, copyleft, source-available) is a keyword-based skim aid, not a legal opinion, exactly as the tool's own front page and footer already say.
